text: The new moon is setting up some excellent tides this weekend, and with northerly winds forecast, water temperatures should continue to climb. The big evening high tides will be ideal for chasing quality whiting up on the flats tight against the mangroves. Fresh yabbies remain hard to beat, so it’s worth getting out early to pump a few on the afternoon low. Beach worms are also proving highly effective and continue to account for plenty of fish. The large afternoon low tides will create plenty of opportunities for flathead anglers, with many of the larger drains becoming accessible as water levels drop. There’s also the chance of encountering threadfin salmon and even the odd barramundi in these areas. Mangrove jacks should be firing on the combination of warm water, larger tides and northerly winds. Soft plastics in the 3-5 inch range worked deep into the snags on the back end of the run-out tide are producing fish. Bream and cod are also active around the same structure. Grunter continue to fish well throughout the creek systems. Prawn-style lures and soft vibes are working nicely, while anglers fishing baits are finding success with strips of squid and mullet. Further afield, reports of school and spotted mackerel have come from around Big Mick and Inskip Point. Traditional trolling methods such as planers rigged with small spoons are working, while small hardbodies in the 80-120mm range are also worth a try.
credit: Coastwatch (Tin Can Bay section by The Chandlery Bait & Tackle)

text: Mackerel continue to dominate catches around Hervey Bay, with plenty of broadbar and school mackerel being caught throughout the region. Whiting are fishing well along the local beaches and across the flats of the Great Sandy Straits. There is also plenty of bait along the Hervey Bay beaches at present, attracting schools of mackerel close to shore. In the Great Sandy Straits, both winter and summer whiting are on the chew, with flathead holding around the creek mouths. Grunter are being caught in the creeks and throughout the Mary River system, while threadfin salmon, blue salmon and barramundi are all active through the straits and local river systems. Mangrove jacks are firing in the western creeks and throughout the Burrum system, where quality grunter and whiting are also being caught in the middle reaches. Offshore, coral trout are biting well on the shallow reefs, while anglers avoiding the sharks are still finding grassy sweetlip and other reef species. Spanish mackerel continue to be caught around Sandy Cape Shoals. Billfish activity is gradually building, with black marlin, striped marlin and yellowfin tuna all being reported from the shelf. The heavy tackle season is showing signs of improvement, although it is still early days. Fraser Island reports remain patchy, while sand crabs are being caught around Waddy Creek and through parts of the straits. text: Fishing has been fairly consistent through the Noosa River this week, with bream the standout species throughout the Noosaville reaches and up towards the First Lake. A couple of quality flathead have also been reported around Tewantin and Goat Island, while plenty of smaller flathead in the 35-40cm range are being caught between the river mouth and Woods Bay on the drift. For bait anglers, prawns and worms continue to be the most reliable options and are accounting for most of the catches. Full Report pending. North Reef continues to produce quality snapper, pearl perch, kingfish and Moses perch. With plenty of current pushing across the wider grounds, the closer reefs are proving the more fishable option at present and are holding plenty of fish. Whale numbers remain high offshore, so boaties should continue to keep a careful lookout when travelling to and from the grounds. Flathead continue to feature strongly in the lower estuary, with good numbers of fish being caught throughout the system. A variety of trevally species are also active through Noosa Sound, providing plenty of action for lure and bait anglers alike. There are still a few queenfish around, although getting them to the boat has been a challenge, with sharks proving a persistent nuisance once fish are hooked.

From the open surf beaches to the sheltered creeks of the Cooloola region, each spot calls for a different approach. That's why local anglers rely on a proper bait fishing store rather than guessing at the servo. text: Weekly Fishing Report: Rainbow Beach & Fraser Island 26 Sept 25. Welcome to this week’s fishing report, where we dive into the latest conditions, catches, and tips to help you make the most of your time on the water. Whether you're heading offshore, beach fishing, or exploring the creeks, we’ve got you covered. Weather and Conditions Last week brought mixed weather, with a few days of southerly winds and a slight temperature drop. Many anglers took advantage of the conditions to fish offshore and along the beaches. Looking ahead, this weekend will see northerly winds—swinging between northeast, northwest, and dead north. While not ideal for offshore fishing, the lack of swell means it’s still possible to get out there and enjoy a productive day. Beach Fishing Highlights The beaches have been buzzing with activity, and there’s plenty to target: Tailor : Reports of good catches, though numbers are higher on the island than the mainland. Whiting, Bream, Tarwhine, and Dart : These species are biting well, especially along Teewah Beach. With plenty of gutter formations, the key is to fish the last two hours of the run-out tide and the first of the run-in. Move frequently to locate the fish—gutter hopping is your best strategy. text: 10 Tips for Mud Crabbing around Rainbow Beach. Catching mud crab in Queensland’s Great Sandy Straits is an exhilarating experience for fishing enthusiasts. Rainbow Beach, strategically located on its southern end offers fishers easy access for both land based and those with their own boat to experience catching the famous QLD “ muddie ”. The pristine waters and diverse mangrove habitats that this beautiful coastal town offers produce some of the tastiest mud crabs in the state. To help you make the most of your mud crabbing adventure, we’ve compiled 10 expert tips that ensure a successful, sustainable, and enjoyable outing. 1. Time Your Trip around the moon phases Timing is everything when it comes to mud crabbing. The best time to go crabbing in Rainbow Beach is the period leading up to the full and new moons. Bigger tides during these periods really get the crabs firing. At this time, crabs are more active and are often visible in the shallow waters, giving you a higher chance of catching them. Keep an eye on tide charts and plan your trip accordingly for maximum success. Although mud crabs are available all year in Rainbow Beach, the peak in numbers occurs from December to March. The best quality (A Grade crab) is caught in the cooler months between April to September 2.
